item.content:encoded:
After close vote, New Zealand must wait weeks for new government Reuters | Updated: 08-11-2026 07:57 IST | Created: 08-11-2026 07:57 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

New Zealanders faced weeks of uncertainty on Sunday over who will govern the country after their general election, with the current coalition holding a slim majority but a potentially decisive slice of votes still to count. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's National Party and its partners ACT and New Zealand First were on track for 67 of the currently projected 131-seat parliament, Electoral Commission preliminary results of Saturday's vote showed. Sixty-six seats are needed for a majority. But special votes, around 14% of the total, remain to be counted, the commission said. These — including ballots from overseas New Zealanders and people voting outside their electorates — have historically favoured the left. They will be announced with the final count on November 27. Until a coalition to govern New Zealand for the next three years is formed, Luxon will head a caretaker government. CENTRIST OPPORTUNITY PARTY MAY PLAY KEY ROLE Neither the prime minister nor opposition leader Chris Hipkins of the Labour Party claimed victory in their speeches following the election, which has been dominated by talk of a soft economy and the cost of living. "I've been saying it's going to be a very tight election — it has definitely proven to be that. We unfortunately don't know what that means for another three weeks," Luxon told a press conference but added that on current numbers it was "quite feasible" that National could build a government with its current partners. If the National-led coalition loses its majority at the official count, either it or a left-leaning coalition would require the support of the centrist Opportunity Party, which looks likely to enter parliament for the first time. Luxon, who had repeatedly ruled out working with Opportunity, softened his stance on Sunday, refusing to again rule the party out and instead saying it would be entirely appropriate to build a relationship with Opportunity, without defining it. Mona Krewel, a senior political science lecturer at Victoria University of Wellington, said she believed it was possible the two parties could work together. "I actually would take them (Opportunity) for very centrist, very pragmatic, and so I do think they could make it work with National," she said. NATIONAL, LABOUR SUPPORT HITS LOW New Zealand adopted a mixed-member proportional system in 1996, in which people vote for both a party and a local constituency candidate. There are 71 constituency, or electorate, seats, and the Electoral Commission now projects there will be 60 party list seats. National and a minor party, Te Pati Maori, each won a disproportionately high share of constituency seats relative to their popular vote support due to tactical voting, reshaping the balance of seats in parliament and sparking debate about the electoral system, said political commentator Ben Thomas. "It certainly looks as if we're on track for the least-proportional parliament that we've had, as a result of the vagaries of the rules around how electorate seats interact with the parliament as a whole," Thomas said. The popular vote shares for National and Labour were each below 30%, their lowest since the new system was introduced, signalling voters' frustration with the slow pace of economic growth under Luxon and a lack of trust in Hipkins' promise to turn things around. National's low popular vote means the party is set to lose several senior lawmakers in the next parliament, including Finance Minister Nicola Willis. Willis remains in the role for the next four weeks. Simeon Brown, a National lawmaker, said the party had lost some significant people, making the result "bittersweet".

item.title: US Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed launches 'Habibi PAC' days after historic election win
item.description: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has launched a political action committee (PAC) named 'Habibi PAC', days after becoming the first Muslim member of the United States Senate, Al Jazeera reported.
item.content:encoded:
US Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed launches 'Habibi PAC' days after historic election win Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has launched a political action committee (PAC) named 'Habibi PAC', days after becoming the first Muslim member of the United States Senate, Al Jazeera reported. ANI | Updated: 07-11-2026 21:32 IST | Created: 07-11-2026 21:32 IST

Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has launched a political action committee (PAC) named 'Habibi PAC', days after becoming the first Muslim member of the United States Senate, Al Jazeera reported. According to Al Jazeera, citing a filing submitted to the Federal Election Commission (FEC) on Thursday, Habibi PAC has been registered as a leadership PAC sponsored by El-Sayed. Such committees operate separately from a politician's own election campaign and are used to raise and spend funds in support of other political candidates and political activities. The name 'Habibi', an Arabic term of endearment meaning 'my dear' or 'my beloved', is a phrase El-Sayed frequently used during his election campaign. He also used the expression while addressing US Vice President JD Vance during his victory speech in Detroit, saying, "JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January." El-Sayed is among several newly elected Democratic lawmakers who have registered leadership PACs following Tuesday's election, according to FEC filings. Others include Arizona Congressman-elect Amish Shah, who registered 'PACStreet Boy', Iowa Senator-elect Josh Turek, who launched 'WheelPAC', and North Carolina Senator-elect Roy Cooper, who registered 'One NC PAC', as reported by Al Jazeera. According to Al Jazeera, citing OpenSecrets, leadership PACs are often used by ambitious lawmakers to build influence among their colleagues and strengthen their prospects of securing party leadership positions or committee chairmanships. They typically contribute to other lawmakers, political parties and political committees. During the 2024 election cycle, leadership PACs contributed USD 79.3 million to federal candidates. While most of the contributions went to Republican candidates, a Democratic leadership PAC emerged as the largest individual donor, Al Jazeera reported, citing OpenSecrets. El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, defeated Republican candidate Mike Rogers following a campaign in which US President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Senator Ted Cruz questioned his loyalty, called him a "jihadist" and attempted to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood movement without providing evidence. Getting money out of politics was among El-Sayed's central campaign pledges. During his victory speech, he highlighted the significance of his electoral success, saying that in a contest between money and the people, "the many can win". His victory came amid the most expensive midterm election on record. According to Al Jazeera, an analysis of FEC data by OpenSecrets noted that total spending in the election cycle is expected to reach USD 11.9 billion, compared with USD 8.9 billion in 2022. Outside spending, largely driven by super PACs, is projected to reach USD 3.9 billion, marking an 85 per cent increase from the 2022 midterm elections. Meanwhile, so-called dark money contributions from donors whose identities are not disclosed have already reached at least USD 1.47 billion, surpassing the previous record of USD 1.35 billion set during the 2024 election cycle, which also included the presidential race. According to Al Jazeera, OpenSecrets found that conservative groups outspent liberal groups by approximately USD 360 million in outside spending, while Democratic candidates were expected to outspend their Republican counterparts by around USD 800 million. Political action committees, or PACs, are organisations that raise and spend money to support or oppose candidates for public office. Leadership PACs, in particular, allow elected officials and lawmakers to support other candidates and political organisations independently of their own campaign committees. (ANI)

item.content:encoded:
X says police order demanding removal of Indian free-speech groups' accounts was fake Reuters | Updated: 06-11-2026 12:37 IST | Created: 06-11-2026 12:37 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Police orders asking X to block online accounts of two of India's most prominent free speech groups were fake, the social media company told an Indian court on Friday, days after the purported content removal requests sparked a public outcry. The orders, submitted through X's online reporting form in the name of a senior Delhi police officer, sought the removal of the accounts of the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) and the Software Freedom Law Centre, India (SFLC.in), claiming they had defamed the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the Hindu nationalist group from which Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party emerged. "It turns out this was somebody playing an impostor, somebody impersonating Delhi police who has sent this," a lawyer for X told the Delhi High Court, saying the company had conducted an internal investigation. Delhi police did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Free-speech activists have repeatedly said that India's strict content removal regulations are a way to curb dissent in the world's most populous nation. India, which has more than 1.1 billion internet subscribers, says the directives target unlawful or misleading content and respect lawful expression. The purported takedown orders invoked Indian rules that require platforms to act on the notices within three hours. X forwarded them to the affected users before establishing that they were fake. IFF had asked the court to quash the orders, which sparked an uproar on social media this week, with Amnesty and India's main opposition party contesting their legality. The groups also received legal notices last week, purportedly on behalf of the RSS, that demanded they stop criticising and documenting government blocking orders, according to the petition.

item.content:encoded:
Trump questions Russian fuel ban, signals no change President Donald Trump questioned the US law banning Russian petroleum imports, stating he would review it, though no policy change was announced amid a dispute over his administration's authorisation of Russian diesel transactions. ANI | Updated: 06-11-2026 10:05 IST | Created: 06-11-2026 10:05 IST

US President Donald Trump (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

President Donald Trump has cast doubt on the US law banning Russian petroleum imports, indicating that he would review the legislation while declaring no policy change amid mounting controversy surrounding his administration’s clearance of Russian diesel transactions. “That probably makes it a pretty bad law. I'll take a look at it, sure,” Trump stated after a journalist informed him that the measure had been enacted by Congress and signed by President Joe Biden in 2022. During his interaction in the Oval Office, the reporter raised questions regarding a vessel transporting Russian diesel across the ocean towards the United States, alongside the legal restrictions governing the offloading of its cargo. Initially, Trump questioned whether the restriction fell under the purview of the Jones Act, prompting the correspondent to clarify that the issue pertained to legislation passed in 2022. His response provided no timeline, proposed amendment or explanation regarding how the administration intended to reconcile its authorisation of diesel imports with the statutory import prohibition, nor did he declare that the ban had been lifted. This distinction remains critical, given that the Treasury had previously granted a separate authorisation roughly four weeks earlier. On October 9, the Office of Foreign Assets Control released General License 135, permitting financial dealings otherwise prohibited under two sets of Russia-related sanctions regulations whenever they involve the sale, delivery, offloading or importation of Russian-origin diesel. The document explicitly covers imports into the United States, with the waiver remaining in effect until 12.01 am Eastern Daylight Time on April 7, 2027. While exempting withdrawals from accounts maintained at US financial institutions belonging to Russia's central bank, National Wealth Fund or Finance Ministry, the licence specifically targets diesel rather than signalling a general reopening of trade encompassing all Russian petroleum products. Conversely, the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, formally approved on April 8, 2022, independently prohibits inbound shipments of Russian products listed under Chapter 27 of the US tariff schedule. The framework outlines a strict protocol for lifting this restriction, requiring presidential certification verifying an agreement accepted by Ukraine regarding Russia's withdrawal and a halt to hostilities, the elimination of any immediate Russian military threat directed at NATO members, and recognition of Ukrainian self-determination. Additionally, the requirement necessitates prior consultation with congressional committees, alongside a 90-day review period following certification before any cancellation takes effect, unless Congress passes a resolution of disapproval. The aforementioned Treasury licence, on its own, does not establish that this statutory process has been fulfilled. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill formally contested the approval through a November 2 letter addressed to port and terminal operators, just three days before Trump's recent comments. “The Trump Administration’s authorisation of Russian fuel imports directly conflicts with federal law,” she asserted. Sherrill contended that the legislation did not grant the executive branch blanket authority to set aside the prohibition through licences, cautioning commercial entities against accepting deliveries of the petroleum and vowing that New Jersey would deploy all available legal and regulatory measures to block such imports. (ANI)
